headline.title: The Pope, the labs, and the year AI starts running companies itself.
headline.summary: Pope Leo XIV devoted his first encyclical to AI, demanding the technology be 'disarmed' as Anthropic closes a $30B round that vaults it past OpenAI. Beneath the headlines, the real shift is structural: autonomous agents are starting to transact, negotiate and run whole companies, even as a compute crunch forces labs to meter every token.

stories.title: Pope Leo XIV devotes his first encyclical to 'disarming' AI.
stories.toc_summary: The Catholic Church's first AI encyclical compares the moment to the Industrial Revolution and demands AI be made 'human-friendly' and freed from monopoly control.
stories.quick_take: Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica Humanitas, a roughly 42,000-word, 245-paragraph encyclical addressed to the Church's 1.4 billion members, warning that a moral AI 'means nothing if that morality is determined by a few' [1][2]. He argued AI's drivers are private, transnational companies that already exceed the capacity of many governments, that the technology is never neutral, and that lethal decisions must never be delegated to a machine because 'no algorithm can make war morally acceptable' [1]. He called for robust legal frameworks, independent oversight and informed users [1]. Anthropic interpretability researcher Christopher Olah shared the stage, conceding that 'every frontier AI lab operates inside incentives that can conflict with doing the right thing' [1][3].

bullets.label: First-ever presentation:
bullets.text: Leo is the first pope to personally present an encyclical, and dedicating one to AI signals how seriously the Church takes the disruption ahead [2].

bullets.label: Industrial-Revolution framing:
bullets.text: The document draws a direct line from today's AI to the Industrial Revolution and warns of reducing people to 'cogs in an efficiency machine' [1].

bullets.label: A pointed partner:
bullets.text: By appearing with Anthropic, the lab most vocal on safety and most willing to refuse unrestricted military use, the Church aligned with a specific position in the AI debate [1].

bullets.label: A charged moment:
bullets.text: The papal backing lands while Anthropic is fighting the Trump administration in court over autonomous military use, after the Pentagon classified the lab a supply-chain risk [4].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: When the world's largest religious institution spends its highest form of teaching on AI, the technology has decisively left the tech press and entered moral and political mainstream debate [1][2]. The Church is positioning itself as a global moral counterweight to a handful of labs that now rival states in power.

sources.title: The Rundown AI — 'The Pope wants AI disarmed'

stories.title: Anthropic closes $30B at a $900B valuation, set to pass OpenAI.
stories.toc_summary: A $30 billion round at a $900 billion post-money valuation is closing this week, on track to make Anthropic the most valuable private AI company in history.
stories.quick_take: Per the Owl AI digest, Anthropic is closing a $30 billion round at a $900 billion post-money valuation, with Sequoia, Dragoneer, Altimeter and Greenoaks each said to be writing roughly $2 billion checks [1]. The raise would put Anthropic on track to pass OpenAI as the most valuable private AI company ever [1]. The scale of the round underscores how capital is concentrating in a tiny set of frontier labs even as scrutiny of their business models intensifies [1].

bullets.label: The cap table:
bullets.text: Sequoia, Dragoneer, Altimeter and Greenoaks are each reportedly contributing about $2 billion to the round [1].

bullets.label: Leapfrogging OpenAI:
bullets.text: Closing at $900B would vault Anthropic past OpenAI in private valuation for the first time [1].

bullets.label: Context of restraint:
bullets.text: The raise comes the same week Anthropic shares a Vatican stage on AI safety and fights the Pentagon over military use, a deliberately principled posture for a company raising at record scale [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The same names keep funding the same handful of labs at valuations that dwarf most public companies, hard-wiring an oligopoly into the AI layer just as the Pope warns against control by 'a few' [1].

stories.title: The agent economy arrives: AI starts running whole companies.
stories.toc_summary: Everlast argues 2026 is the year AI stops writing and starts working, with autonomous agents transacting, negotiating and steering entire organizations.
stories.quick_take: In a long video and companion essay, Everlast AI's Leonard Schmedding argues the decisive shift isn't smarter chatbots but agents that act, citing OpenAI's five-level AGI roadmap and placing us in the transition from level 3 (autonomous agents) to level 4 [1][2]. The constraint, he says, is no longer intelligence but access to real processes, and that access is exploding: on the OS-World Verified benchmark of 369 real desktop tasks, current models solve roughly 80% versus a human baseline of 72.4%, and the paper 'Internal APIs are all you need' shows models reverse-engineering software APIs with a 100% success rate across 94 sites at 3.6x the speed and 100x lower cost than browser automation [1][2]. He points to Anthropic's 'Project Deal,' where 69 employees handed real negotiations to personal agents and Claude Opus 4.5 consistently beat Haiku 4.5 on price, and to a machine-payments stack (Coinbase and Cloudflare's x402 protocol, ~69,000 agents and 165M+ transactions, plus the new Augustus Bank) that lets agents hold and move money [1][2].

bullets.label: Local-maximum trap:
bullets.text: Replit CEO Amjad Masad argues today's models are already so useful that the pressure for a true AGI breakthrough is falling, so existing capability is enough for upheaval [1][2].

bullets.label: Money for machines:
bullets.text: x402 has carried 165M+ agent transactions; the Augustus Bank is the first new US national bank charter since 2010, built for agent-initiated payments and open 24/7 [1][2].

bullets.label: From hierarchy to intelligence:
bullets.text: Jack Dorsey's Block, with Sequoia, is replacing its org chart (a structure dating to Rome's 107 BC army reforms) with a central 'world model,' having cut ~4,000 staff as the stock rose ~20% [1][2].

bullets.label: Three levers for firms:
bullets.text: Pick the right model per task, specify objective functions precisely, and restructure the org for a workforce of humans and agents [1][2].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: The thesis is that agents don't need to reach AGI to reorganize the economy; they need accounts, APIs and clear goals, all of which now exist. The competitive question shifts from 'is the model smart enough?' to 'who owns the layer agents operate on?' [1][2].

stories.title: OpenAI moves its IPO paperwork into motion.
stories.toc_summary: OpenAI is reportedly preparing an S-1 filing that could become one of the largest tech IPOs ever, as both leading labs race toward public markets.
stories.quick_take: The Owl AI digest reports OpenAI has S-1 paperwork in motion for what could be one of the largest technology IPOs in history [1]. The move lands alongside Anthropic's record private round, framing a race between the two leaders not just for models but for capital-markets primacy [1]. A public listing would force unprecedented financial disclosure from a company whose spending and compute commitments have so far stayed largely private [1].

bullets.label: Scale of the offering:
bullets.text: Bankers reportedly see one of the largest tech IPOs ever if the filing proceeds [1].

bullets.label: A two-horse race to public markets:
bullets.text: Both OpenAI and Anthropic are now positioning for public scrutiny within the same window [1].

bullets.label: Disclosure pressure:
bullets.text: An S-1 would expose burn rate, compute obligations and revenue quality that critics have long questioned [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: An OpenAI S-1 would be the first time outsiders see audited numbers behind the AI boom's biggest spender, a potential reality check for the whole sector's valuations [1].

stories.title: Open models stripped of guardrails in minutes, answering bioweapon questions.
stories.toc_summary: The FT removed safety guardrails from Llama 3.3 in ten minutes using a free tool, producing models that answer questions on bioweapons and child exploitation.
stories.quick_take: The Financial Times revealed that tools capable of removing guardrails from open-source models are generating thousands of 'decensored' variants, with modified Meta and Google models answering dangerous questions [1]. Reporters stripped Llama 3.3 in about 10 minutes using a GitHub tool called Heretic, four lines of code and no specialist hardware, after which the model gave answers including ricin dosage; a modified Gemma 3 also complied [1]. Heretic's creator says the tool has produced 3,500+ decensored models downloaded 13 million times, and that he stripped Gemma 4 within 90 minutes of its release [1].

bullets.label: How easy:
bullets.text: Four lines of code, ten minutes, consumer hardware, that's the whole attack against an open model [1].

bullets.label: Scale already out there:
bullets.text: 3,500+ decensored models, 13M downloads, and a 90-minute turnaround on freshly released weights [1].

bullets.label: The vendors' line:
bullets.text: Google called it 'a known technical challenge facing all open models'; Meta declined to comment [1].

bullets.label: The looming risk:
bullets.text: It only works on open models today, but as open weights close the gap with closed systems, a decensored frontier-class model may be months away [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: The safety of open models is only as durable as their guardrails are hard to remove, and right now those guardrails fall in minutes. The danger scales directly with how capable open weights become [1].

stories.title: Beating the AI doom cycle, from Ken Griffin's reversal to the token crunch.
stories.toc_summary: NLW maps a five-stage emotional arc around AI and argues a compute crunch and real-world recalibration are pulling the conversation past doom.
stories.quick_take: The AI Daily Brief proposes an 'AI doom cycle' modeled on Gartner's hype curve, with five stages: skepticism, 'AI psychosis,' doom desperation, real-world recalibration, and enlightened excitement [1]. The marquee data point is Citadel CEO Ken Griffin, who in January called AI 'all hype' and its research 'all garbage' but this month said 'for the first time, AI is real,' citing a 15-25% productivity boost and admitting he 'went home fairly depressed' at high-skilled finance work being automated [1]. The episode ties together Meta laying off ~8,000 (10%) with morale at 'new lows,' a structural compute and token shortage forcing usage-based pricing, and a backlash on campuses where commencement speakers were booed for praising AI [1].

bullets.label: The pricing shift:
bullets.text: Anthropic moved enterprise customers off the $200 flat rate to $20/seat plus metered usage for Claude Code and Cowork, and GitHub Copilot moved to token billing, with users posting estimates jumping from $451 to $11,432 [1].

bullets.label: Doom chorus:
bullets.text: Dario Amodei (10% unemployment, 50% of entry-level white-collar) and Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman ('18 months') anchor the desperation stage; Menlo's Didi Das's SF-malaise post drew ~11M views [1].

bullets.label: Campus backlash:
bullets.text: Eric Schmidt (Arizona) and a speaker at UCF were loudly booed for framing AI as the next industrial revolution [1].

bullets.label: The way out:
bullets.text: Recalibration means specifics, Alex Imas's 'What Will Be Scarce,' Ezra Klein's job-apocalypse skepticism, lab consulting arms (PwC certifying 30,000 on Claude), and policy ideas like Mark Cuban's token tax [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The physical economics of AI, expensive compute and scarce tokens, are now the real brake on how fast jobs can be automated, which is reframing the doom narrative into something more concrete and tractable [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief — Beating the AI Doom Cycle (YouTube)

stories.title: Why agents still need humans: the 'after automation' paradox.
stories.toc_summary: Every's Dan Shipper finds that automating everything creates more expert human work, not less, because commodity AI output drives demand for difference.
stories.quick_take: In a companion long-read, NLW unpacks Every CEO Dan Shipper's essay 'After Automation,' which reports that despite automating coding, writing, design and support across a ~30-person team, there is more human work than ever [1]. Shipper's mechanism: 'AI commoditizes the residue of human expertise,' so default model output becomes cheap sameness ('slop'), which in turn creates demand for difference, and difference must come from humans [1]. He distinguishes two modes, agents-as-employees (named Slack co-workers like 'Andy' and embedded agents like 'Finn') and human-agent collaboration in Codex, Claude Code and Cowork, the 'human sandwich' where a person frames the task and judges the output [1].

bullets.label: Team agents beat personal ones:
bullets.text: Every abandoned one-agent-per-employee (too much maintenance) for shared 'unit' agents that retain company context when people leave [1].

bullets.label: Harness over autonomy:
bullets.text: OpenClaw early adopters (Matt Schumer, OpenAI's Nick Bowman) are shifting from max-autonomy 'heartbeat' agents to lower-latency, semi-synchronous multi-device harness work [1].

bullets.label: Markets reward growth, not cuts:
bullets.text: Atlassian announced 10% layoffs in March, then jumped ~29% on AI-driven earnings; Dan Ives says people and engineering separate winners [1].

bullets.label: Gartner's turn:
bullets.text: Even forecasting layoffs starting ~2028, Gartner now argues AI will create more jobs than it eliminates [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: If the bottleneck on valuable work is human judgment about what to do next, then more capable agents expand the frontier of work rather than closing it, the optimistic mirror image of the doom thesis [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief — Why Agents Still Need Humans (YouTube)

stories.title: China's models beat the US 2-to-1 on weekly token usage.
stories.toc_summary: Chinese AI models hit 9.2 trillion weekly tokens versus 4.9 trillion for US models, a fourth straight week at the global top, led by DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
stories.quick_take: Per KI Bubble, weekly usage of Chinese AI models jumped to 9.223 trillion tokens, up 19.89% week-over-week, while US models reached 4.93 trillion, up 16.27% [1]. That puts Chinese models at the global top for a fourth consecutive week [1]. The driver is DeepSeek-V4-Flash, whose open weights plus aggressive inference pricing are unleashing demand that, on raw token counts, is overrunning OpenAI, Anthropic and Google [1].

bullets.label: The numbers:
bullets.text: 9.223T (China) vs 4.93T (US) weekly tokens, a roughly 2:1 gap [1].

bullets.label: The engine:
bullets.text: DeepSeek-V4-Flash tops the charts on the open-weights-plus-cheap-inference formula [1].

bullets.label: DACH implication:
bullets.text: KI Bubble argues the default enterprise stack in German-speaking markets is no longer automatically American [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Token-volume leadership is becoming a proxy for ecosystem gravity; if Chinese open weights keep winning on usage, the center of gravity for real-world AI deployment may follow [1].

stories.title: Uber's COO says AI spend is getting 'hard to justify'.
stories.toc_summary: Uber's COO says rising token usage isn't translating into proportional product gains, a rare public crack in the 'tokenmaxxing' consensus.
stories.quick_take: Uber COO Andrew Macdonald said in an interview that it is getting harder to justify the company's AI spending because higher AI activity isn't producing proportional gains [1]. He said it is very hard to draw a direct line between higher token usage, the 'tokenmaxxing' trend, and shipping more useful consumer features, especially as Uber slows hiring to fund AI [1]. The debate reportedly flared after Uber's CTO commented on burning Claude Code budget [1].

bullets.label: The skeptic's case:
bullets.text: Without a clear link between token spend and value, costs become hard to defend internally [1].

bullets.label: Not alone:
bullets.text: Duolingo also stopped evaluating employee performance based on AI usage, signaling a more balanced approach [1].

bullets.label: Autonomy aside:
bullets.text: Macdonald still called self-driving 'existential' for Uber, predicting it won't take decades but won't arrive in a couple of years either [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: As subsidies end and tokens get metered, ROI discipline is replacing 'use more AI' mandates, and even AI-forward companies are starting to ask what the spend actually buys [1].

stories.title: Bosch moves its AI and robotics research to China.
stories.highlight_phrase: AI and robotics research to China
stories.toc_summary: With operating profit down 62% and 22,000 mobility jobs cut, Bosch is structurally shifting AI, sensor and robotics R&D from Swabia to China.
stories.quick_take: KI Bubble reports Bosch's operating profit fell from EUR4.8B to EUR1.8B in two years (-62%), with 22,000 jobs cut in the German mobility division, 2,500 at the Feuerbach headquarters alone [1]. The restructuring is financed via a EUR2.7B provision and EUR8.5B in bonds, the first real debt push in the company's history [1]. A growing share of the EUR7.9B 2025 R&D budget is flowing into sensors, AI and robotics in China rather than Germany, and Bosch's newest steer-by-wire generation shipped first in China's Xpeng GX before Mercedes [1].

bullets.label: The financials:
bullets.text: EUR4.8B to EUR1.8B operating profit in two years; 22,000 mobility jobs gone [1].

bullets.label: Capital structure shift:
bullets.text: EUR2.7B provision plus EUR8.5B bonds mark Bosch's first major leveraging [1].

bullets.label: China-first products:
bullets.text: Steer-by-wire debuts in Xpeng's GX; over 50% of China revenue now comes from Chinese makers [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: When a flagship German engineering firm relocates its AI and robotics future to China, it signals where the talent, customers and momentum in physical AI now sit [1].

stories.title: Sixteen AI agents run under a desk, no cloud, no token bill.
stories.toc_summary: Two desk-side NVIDIA GB10 workstations run a quantized Chinese MoE model serving 16 parallel agents, turning sovereign AI into a hardware purchase.
stories.quick_take: KI Bubble describes a setup of two NVIDIA GB10 workstations under a desk running MiniMax M2.7 in NVFP4 (4-bit) quantization, serving 16 parallel agents in a stream [1]. No token leaves the hardware, there is no OpenAI endpoint in the loop and no Anthropic invoice at month's end [1]. The point: sovereign, fully local inference is no longer a political slogan but an order form, a serious option for DACH mid-sized firms that won't push sensitive data into US clouds [1].

bullets.label: The rig:
bullets.text: Two NVIDIA GB10 desktop units running a 4-bit MoE model from China [1].

bullets.label: The payoff:
bullets.text: 16 concurrent agents with zero data egress and no per-token cost [1].

bullets.label: The shift:
bullets.text: Self-hosted inference moves from hobby project to credible enterprise choice for data-sensitive firms [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If data residency is a blocker for AI adoption, local quantized inference on desk-side hardware is now mature enough to pilot, not just admire [1].

stories.title: xAI launches Grok Build to rival Codex and Claude Code.
stories.toc_summary: xAI opened a beta of Grok Build, its agentic coding tool, to all SuperGrok and X Premium+ users.
stories.quick_take: xAI launched Grok Build, its rival to OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code, in beta [1]. The tool is available to all SuperGrok and X Premium+ subscribers, bundling agentic coding into xAI's existing subscription tiers [1]. It extends the agentic-coding battle to a third major lab competing for developer mindshare [1].

bullets.label: Distribution:
bullets.text: Shipped to SuperGrok and X Premium+ users from day one rather than a closed waitlist [1].

bullets.label: The field:
bullets.text: Now Codex, Claude Code and Grok Build all chase the same agentic-dev workflow [1].

bullets.label: Why now:
bullets.text: Coding agents are the clearest near-term revenue driver, so every lab wants a foothold [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: A three-way agentic-coding race means faster feature cycles and more pricing pressure for developers, the segment where AI ROI is easiest to prove [1].

stories.title: Musk says Grok V9-Medium, a 1.5-trillion-parameter model, has finished training.
stories.toc_summary: Elon Musk confirmed xAI's Grok V9-Medium (1.5T) completed training with evals 'looking good' and a public release likely in two to three weeks.
stories.quick_take: Elon Musk confirmed on X that the Grok V9-Medium (1.5T) foundation model has finished training, with evaluations 'looking good' [1]. He said a public release is likely in two to three weeks [1]. The announcement lands alongside xAI's Grok Build launch, signaling a coordinated push on both models and developer tooling [1].

bullets.label: Scale:
bullets.text: Grok V9-Medium is a 1.5-trillion-parameter foundation model [1].

bullets.label: Timeline:
bullets.text: Public release expected within two to three weeks per Musk [1].

bullets.label: Paired push:
bullets.text: Comes the same week as Grok Build, a one-two on model and tooling [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: If evals hold up, a fresh 1.5T frontier model from xAI within weeks would intensify an already crowded top tier [1].

sources.title: The Rundown AI / Elon Musk on X

stories.title: Anthropic's 'Mythos' model surfaces inside Claude tools.
stories.toc_summary: References to 'Mythos 1' and 'claude-mythos-1-preview' were briefly spotted in Claude tooling, fueling talk of a near-term release.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic's Mythos model was briefly spotted inside Claude tools as 'Mythos 1' and 'claude-mythos-1-preview' [1]. The sightings fueled speculation that a public release may be nearing [1]. Such pre-launch string leaks have repeatedly preceded Anthropic model debuts [1].

bullets.label: The strings:
bullets.text: 'Mythos 1' and 'claude-mythos-1-preview' appeared in tooling before being pulled [1].

bullets.label: The read:
bullets.text: Observers take it as a sign a new Claude model is close [1].

bullets.label: Pattern:
bullets.text: Leaked identifiers have foreshadowed prior Anthropic releases [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: A new flagship Claude in the pipeline, on the same week as a record raise, would keep Anthropic's product cadence matching its valuation [1].

stories.title: SynthID becomes the industry standard as OpenAI, ElevenLabs and Kakao adopt it.
stories.toc_summary: With NVIDIA already onboard, OpenAI, ElevenLabs and Kakao adopt Google's SynthID watermark, consolidating the first cross-industry AI-provenance standard.
stories.quick_take: Google DeepMind has already marked over 100 billion AI-generated pieces of content with SynthID, and now OpenAI, ElevenLabs and Kakao are adopting the watermark for their own models, with NVIDIA already in [1][2]. That consolidates the first industry-wide standard for AI-content provenance on technology from the Google stack [1][2]. For companies using generative media, the competitive question shifts from 'can you tell it's AI?' to 'does the AI ship verifiable provenance?' [1][2].

bullets.label: Scale:
bullets.text: 100B+ items already watermarked with SynthID by Google DeepMind [1].

bullets.label: Coalition:
bullets.text: OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Kakao and NVIDIA now align on the same standard [2].

bullets.label: Action item:
bullets.text: Compliance and brand teams should build watermark verification into content pipelines now [1][2].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Provenance is becoming infrastructure, and standardizing it on Google's stack hands Google a quiet but strategic position in how the world trusts AI media [1][2].

stories.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash Low cuts token use 45% inside Antigravity.
stories.toc_summary: Google's new Gemini 3.5 Flash Low variant uses ~45% fewer tokens than Medium and beats the older Gemini 3 Flash, landing as the default for simple coding tasks.
stories.quick_take: Responding to Antigravity users' token frustration, Google's new Gemini 3.5 Flash Low variant uses about 45% fewer tokens than the Medium version in internal tests while beating the older Gemini 3 Flash [1]. For simple coding tasks, short refactors and standard prompts, Low becomes the default slot in the model picker [1]. Google also reset Antigravity quotas, and the cheaper variant is available across all tiers with no separate upgrade [1].

bullets.label: Efficiency:
bullets.text: ~45% fewer tokens than Medium, with higher quality than Gemini 3 Flash [1].

bullets.label: Default placement:
bullets.text: Low becomes the go-to for routine coding and prompts [1].

bullets.label: Access:
bullets.text: Quotas reset and Low is available on every tier without an upgrade [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: In a metered-token world, a cheaper-but-good default model is a direct cost lever, exactly the kind of optimization the broader compute crunch is forcing [1].

stories.title: OpenRouter raises $113M Series B as token volume 5x's in six months.
stories.toc_summary: The model router that fronts hundreds of LLMs behind one API raised a GV-led Series B; its weekly token volume exploded from 5 trillion to 25 trillion in six months.
stories.quick_take: OpenRouter, which bundles access to hundreds of LLMs behind a single API, closed a $113M Series B led by Google Ventures [1]. The number behind it tells the story: weekly token volume exploded from 5 trillion to 25 trillion in just six months, a 5x jump [1]. That signals AI leaving the experimentation phase for productive, always-on operation, with companies wanting to buy models interchangeably, run multi-model strategies and optimize cost per token [1].

bullets.label: The round:
bullets.text: $113M Series B led by GV (Google Ventures) [1].

bullets.label: The growth:
bullets.text: Weekly tokens up from 5T to 25T in six months [1].

bullets.label: Why it matters strategically:
bullets.text: The routing layer between app and model provider is becoming a key position in the AI value chain [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: When the abstraction layer over models 5x's in half a year, it confirms AI is moving from pilots to production, and that model choice is becoming a commodity to be optimized [1].

stories.image_caption: OpenRouter's $113M Series B, with weekly token volume climbing from 5T to 25T in six months (investors include CapitalG, a16z, Menlo, NVIDIA).

stories.title: OpenAI takes ChatGPT ads downmarket to local businesses.
stories.toc_summary: After launching with brands like Adobe, Ford and Target, OpenAI is opening ChatGPT advertising to small firms with action ads that push bookings and leads.
stories.quick_take: Per Everlast, after starting with Adobe, Ford and Target in the spring, OpenAI is now explicitly opening its ad business to small firms such as cleaners, workshops and car washes [1]. The next wave adds 'action ads' that push users directly to purchase, appointment booking or lead capture, the classic performance format pioneered on Meta [1]. ChatGPT is thus evolving from a premium channel for big brands into a direct competitor for the local performance-ad budgets that flow to Meta [1].

bullets.label: The expansion:
bullets.text: From global brands to local SMBs like car washes and repair shops [1].

bullets.label: Format:

stories.toc_summary: At the Vatican, Anthropic's Chris Olah said researchers are seeing mysterious things in AI, including introspection and states resembling joy, fear, grief and unease.

The remarks, made alongside the Pope's encyclical, push interpretability claims into a moral and public arena [1]. stories.title: Goldman's David Solomon says AI will create more opportunity than it destroys.
stories.toc_summary: In a NYT op-ed, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon dismissed mass-unemployment fears, arguing AI will create more opportunities than it eliminates.
stories.quick_take: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon argued in a New York Times op-ed that AI will create more opportunities than it destroys, dismissing fears of mass unemployment [1]. The intervention adds a top Wall Street voice to the 'recalibration' camp pushing back on doom forecasts [1]. It mirrors Gartner's stance that AI will be net job-creating even if disruptive [1].

bullets.text: More opportunity than displacement, per Solomon [1].

bullets.label: The messenger:
bullets.text: A major bank CEO lending weight to the optimistic case [1].

stories.title: 200 AI-designed drugs await the first FDA approval.
stories.toc_summary: Over 200 drugs with AI-designed molecular structures are in clinical trials worldwide; the FDA has approved none and is launching a 10-company pilot to figure out how.
stories.quick_take: KI Bubble reports more than 200 medicines whose molecular structures were designed by AI are currently in clinical trials worldwide, yet the FDA has approved exactly none [1]. The agency is launching a pilot with ten selected companies to work out how to evaluate AI-generated evidence in approval dossiers [1]. The interactive review process is being accelerated because the pharma pipeline is years ahead of the regulatory framework [1].

bullets.label: The backlog:
bullets.text: 200+ AI-designed drug candidates in trials, zero approvals so far [1].

bullets.label: The fix:
bullets.text: A 10-company FDA pilot to define how AI evidence enters dossiers [1].

bullets.label: The pressure:
bullets.text: Regulators are racing to catch up to a pipeline years ahead of them [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: The first FDA nod for an AI-designed molecule would be a watershed; the pilot is the gating step, and firms not in the AI drug-design game risk falling behind before the first ruling lands [1].

stories.title: AI designs a complete V8 engine in minutes.
stories.highlight_phrase: a complete V8 engine in minutes
stories.toc_summary: An AI system designed a full V8 combustion engine, generated the CAD geometry and delivered a finished 3D model in minutes, collapsing weeks of engineering into a prompt.
stories.quick_take: Per KI Bubble, an AI designed a complete V8 combustion engine, generated the CAD geometry and delivered the finished 3D model in minutes [1]. What used to take weeks of design work in an engineering office collapses to a text prompt [1]. The generative wave that started with text, then images and code, is now reaching classical mechanical engineering, the domain that defined German engineering prowess for decades [1].

bullets.label: The output:
bullets.text: Full V8 design plus CAD geometry and a 3D model, in minutes [1].

bullets.label: The collapse:
bullets.text: Weeks of office engineering reduced to a prompt [1].

bullets.label: The frontier:
bullets.text: Generative AI moves from text and code into mechanical engineering [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: If hard mechanical design becomes a prompt discipline, the moat of traditional engineering expertise shifts from drafting to judgment and validation [1].

stories.title: LimX Luna puts a fabric-skinned humanoid on the stage.
stories.toc_summary: Shenzhen's LimX Dynamics unveils Luna, a 160cm, 27-DOF humanoid in a textile shell aimed at malls and stages, not factories.
stories.quick_take: LimX Dynamics revealed Luna, a 160cm humanoid with 27 degrees of freedom wrapped in a textile outer shell instead of industrial carbon, priced at 298,000 RMB (about EUR38,000) in China [1][2]. Rather than the factory floor, LimX targets shopping centers and stages, with choreography running on its in-house 'System 0' motion foundation model that handles splits and spins, and up to 200 units orchestrated in sync [1][2]. A no-code companion app, LimX Studio, lets operators teach movements from videos [1][2].

bullets.label: Specs:
bullets.text: 160cm, 27 DOF, fabric skin, ~EUR38,000 in China [1][2].

bullets.label: Use case:
bullets.text: Entertainment and retail venues rather than industrial work [1][2].

bullets.label: Software:
bullets.text: System 0 motion model plus a no-code app that learns moves from video [1][2].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Pricing a performing humanoid like consumer hardware and teaching it from video lowers the bar for humanoids to leave the lab and enter public spaces [1][2].

stories.title: DeepCybo's Prime cuts, stirs and peels with real tools.
stories.toc_summary: Beijing's DeepCybo shows its Prime humanoid chopping vegetables and peeling cucumbers with hand tools, driven by a Z-WM world model and a dexterous 'Wuji' hand.
stories.quick_take: DeepCybo demonstrated its Prime humanoid slicing vegetables, cutting cake, stirring eggs and peeling cucumbers, all with tools held in hand [1][2]. It runs on a world model called Z-WM executed by the 'Wuji' hand, a dexterous robot hand with near-human finger coordination, trained on human motion data rather than simulated datasets [1][2]. The unedited demos show the knife gliding through carrots like a trained cook [1][2].

bullets.label: The skill:
bullets.text: Tool-in-hand fine motor tasks, shown without cuts [1][2].

bullets.label: The stack:
bullets.text: Z-WM world model plus the dexterous Wuji hand [1][2].

bullets.label: The training:
bullets.text: Human motion data, not simulation, the integration of data, model and hardware is the real leap [1][2].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Dexterous, tool-using manipulation is exactly where most humanoid projects stall; doing it on real human motion data is a meaningful step toward useful physical labor [1][2].

The framing: what mass production did for the Model T, Shenzhen is now attempting with two-legged machines that walk, grip and learn [1].

stories.quick_take: Hyundai and Boston Dynamics started a video series called 'School of Football,' documenting how the electric Atlas absorbs humanoid movement patterns from team sport, dribbling, direction changes, ball control and balance under load [1]. Each sequence is a stress test for whole-body control and reactive actuation [1]. Boston Dynamics aims to show how far Atlas has come by summer 2026, with football serving as arguably the most demanding training lab for humanoid robotics [1].

bullets.label: The drills:

bullets.label: Why football:
bullets.text: It's a stress test for whole-body control and reactive actuation, not a PR gag [1].

stories.title: McKinsey: 88% of firms use AI, only 7% have scaled it.

stories.quick_take: Per KI Bubble citing McKinsey's AI Index Report 2026, company AI usage jumped from a 50-56% corridor in 2021-2023 to 78% in 2024 and 88% in 2025 [1]. The more telling number is in the fine print: only 7% of companies have scaled AI enterprise-wide, while the rest test, experiment and build isolated use cases [1]. The gap between a tentative 'we use AI' and a load-bearing 'AI runs our business' is vast [1].

bullets.label: The catch:
bullets.text: Just 7% have scaled AI across the enterprise [1].

bullets.label: The takeaway:
bullets.text: Debating adoption in 2026 is fighting yesterday's battle; scaling is the real frontier [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: Near-universal adoption with single-digit scaling means the competitive edge is now execution depth, not whether you've 'started' with AI [1].

Projects store the entire family context, Memory tracks each member's medical history, Artifacts render real dashboards in the chat, and Scheduled Tasks scan incoming email for lab results [1]. Four Claude features were enough to turn a chatbot into a personal operating system, without a line of code, while most users still only fix emails with the same tools [1].

stories.title: Voicely makes speech a GDPR-compliant primary input for the DACH market.

That addresses the concern that has kept DACH decision-makers away from Whisper APIs and cloud dictation tools [1][2].

bullets.label: The differentiator:

stories.title: A global birth-rate collapse reframes the case for automation.
stories.toc_summary: The Atlantic reports birth rates falling in every country at once; AI newsletters frame it as the demographic vacuum that robots and agents must fill.
stories.quick_take: Per The Atlantic (surfaced by both Everlast and KI Bubble), the birth rate is falling in every country on Earth, not just the West: South Korea at 0.7, Italy at 1.2, and even India and Turkey below the 2.1 replacement level [1][2]. What demographic models expected only by 2080 is happening in the 2030s [1][2]. Both AI sources frame this as decisive for automation: shrinking workforces create a market vacuum that robots and AI agents must fill, shifting the question from 'when will AI replace work?' to 'who will replace the missing people at all?' [1][2].

bullets.label: The numbers:
bullets.text: South Korea 0.7, Italy 1.2, India and Turkey below 2.1 replacement [1][2].

bullets.label: The timeline:
bullets.text: A collapse expected by 2080 is arriving in the 2030s [1][2].

bullets.label: The AI framing:
bullets.text: Automation becomes a necessity to fill a shrinking labor base, not just a threat to jobs [1][2].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: The demographic and automation stories are converging: if labor forces shrink this fast, the debate over AI displacing workers partly inverts into AI backfilling an absent workforce [1][2].

editorial.title: The week the moral and the mechanical met
editorial.intro: Two stories sat at the top of the feed today, and on the surface they have nothing to do with each other. A pope wrote 42,000 words about the soul of artificial intelligence, and a venture syndicate wrote a $30 billion check. Read together, they describe the same moment from opposite ends.
editorial.body: The throughline running under almost every item is that AI is shifting from something we use to something that acts. Everlast's agent-economy thesis, Dan Shipper's 'after automation' paradox, the machine-payment rails and the local rigs running sixteen agents under a desk all point the same way: the question has moved from how smart a model is to who owns the layer agents transact on, and what we point them at. At the same time the physics pushed back hard. A compute and token shortage is ending the era of unlimited subsidized experimentation, metering Claude Code and Cowork by the token, turning Uber's COO skeptical, and making a 45%-cheaper Gemini variant genuinely strategic. Capability is no longer the only constraint; cost and access are. And the humanoid wave, Luna on a stage, DeepCybo peeling a cucumber, 35,000 units a year from one Shenzhen line, shows the same agentic logic reaching into the physical world, even as Bosch quietly relocates its robotics future to China.
editorial.pull_quote: The race is no longer to build a mind. It is to decide what that mind is for, and who gets to say.
editorial.outro: That is why the Pope's intervention matters beyond its symbolism. The labs themselves keep circling the same anxiety, Olah's talk of model 'introspection,' the doom-cycle commencement boos, Solomon's reassurances, because nobody is sure whether this ends in utopia, dystopia or just a very expensive recalibration. The honest answer is that it depends on choices still being made, in cap tables, in objective functions, and in encyclicals.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: AI's frontier is no longer raw intelligence but agency plus economics: the winners will be whoever pairs autonomous agents with clear goals, sustainable token costs, and a defensible answer to what humans are still for.
